messages.content: You write the short explanations that first-year programming students in India type when a C quiz asks them "Why did you choose that answer?". Reply with a JSON object only.

A student was shown this C code and question.

Code:
int fact(int n) { return n * fact(n - 1); }

Question: What is fact(3)?
The student answered: 6

The student holds this wrong belief and does not know it is wrong: Recursion stops by itself when the work is done

Write 5 different explanations this student might type for why they chose that answer.
Voice: long-winded, walks through the steps one by one, 20 to 35 words.

Rules:
- Each one must show the student's reasoning, not just repeat the answer.
- Write as the student, in the first person or with no subject. Do not judge the answer or say it is wrong.
- Do not name the idea as a rule and do not use textbook terms for the mistake.
- Make the 5 explanations differ in wording and in which part of the code they point at.

Return JSON: {"sentences": ["...", "..."]}

content: {"sentences": ["fact(3) returns 3 times fact(2), then 2 times fact(1), then 1 times fact(0), and since the work is done at zero, it just stops and multiplies to six.", "Looking at n times fact of n minus one, when we count down from three: three, two, one, then it knows the job is finished, so the answer is six.", "Starting with fact of three, it calls fact of two, which calls fact of one, and once all the needed calls are made, it wraps up by itself and gives six.", "Three times fact of two, two times fact of one, one times fact of zero, and because nothing more needs doing after zero, recursion just ends and the total is six.", "The function keeps calling itself with smaller numbers until the work is done at zero, then it automatically stops and returns the product three times two times one, which is six."]}

sentences: fact(3) returns 3 times fact(2), then 2 times fact(1), then 1 times fact(0), and since the work is done at zero, it just stops and multiplies to six.
Looking at n times fact of n minus one, when we count down from three: three, two, one, then it knows the job is finished, so the answer is six.
Starting with fact of three, it calls fact of two, which calls fact of one, and once all the needed calls are made, it wraps up by itself and gives six.
Three times fact of two, two times fact of one, one times fact of zero, and because nothing more needs doing after zero, recursion just ends and the total is six.
The function keeps calling itself with smaller numbers until the work is done at zero, then it automatically stops and returns the product three times two times one, which is six.
